questions.enonce_markdown: (i) Solve, for $\theta$, in the range $0^\circ\le\theta\le180^\circ$, the equation $1-2\sin^2\theta=\cos\theta$. *[3 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
Use the double-angle identity $1-2\sin^2\theta=2\cos^2\theta-1$ (that is $\cos2\theta$):

$$2\cos^2\theta-1=\cos\theta\ \Longrightarrow\ 2\cos^2\theta-\cos\theta-1=0\ \Longrightarrow\ (2\cos\theta+1)(\cos\theta-1)=0.$$

- $\cos\theta=1$ gives $\theta=0^\circ$;
- $\cos\theta=-\dfrac12$ gives $\theta=120^\circ$ (in $0^\circ\le\theta\le180^\circ$ the only angle with cosine $-\frac12$).

Check: $\theta=120^\circ$: $1-2\sin^2120^\circ=1-2\cdot\frac34=-\frac12=\cos120^\circ$. $\theta=0^\circ$: $1-0=1=\cos0^\circ$.

**$\theta=0^\circ$ or $\theta=120^\circ$.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
Taking 1 cm to represent $\dfrac{\pi}{6}$ radian units on the $x$-axis and 2 cm to represent 1 unit on the $y$-axis,

(b) draw the graph of $y=f(x)$. *[2 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Scale.** $x$-axis: $1$ cm for $\frac{\pi}{6}$, so $0$ to $2\pi$ is $12$ cm (mark every $\frac{\pi}{6}$). $y$-axis: $2$ cm per unit, from $-2$ to $2$ (8 cm).

**Points to plot** (from the completed table): $(0,1.7)$, $(\frac{\pi}{6},1)$, $(\frac{\pi}{3},0)$, $(\frac{\pi}{2},-1)$, $(\frac{2\pi}{3},-1.7)$, $(\frac{5\pi}{6},-2)$, $(\pi,-1.7)$, $(\frac{7\pi}{6},-1)$, $(\frac{4\pi}{3},0)$, $(\frac{3\pi}{2},1)$, $(\frac{5\pi}{3},1.7)$, $(\frac{11\pi}{6},2)$, $(2\pi,1.7)$.

Join them with a **smooth curve**: it is a cosine wave of amplitude $2$ (since $\sqrt3\cos x-\sin x=2\cos\left(x+\frac{\pi}{6}\right)$), starting at $1.7$, crossing the $x$-axis at $\frac{\pi}{3}$ and $\frac{4\pi}{3}$, with a minimum $-2$ at $x=\frac{5\pi}{6}$ and a maximum $2$ at $x=\frac{11\pi}{6}$.

questions.enonce_markdown:
From the graph or otherwise,

(c) write down the maximum value of $f(x)$. *[1 mark]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
Write $\sqrt3\cos x-\sin x=R\cos(x+\alpha)$ with $R=\sqrt{(\sqrt3)^2+1^2}=2$ and $\tan\alpha=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt3}$, so $\alpha=\dfrac{\pi}{6}$. Hence $f(x)=2\cos\left(x+\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right)$, whose largest value is $2$, reached when $x+\frac{\pi}{6}=2\pi$, i.e. $x=\frac{11\pi}{6}$, which is inside $0\le x\le2\pi$ (this agrees with the table).

**Maximum value of $f(x)=2$.**
